steps.body: You already know √16 = 4, since 4² = 16. But SOLVING the equation x² = 16 asks something slightly bigger: which numbers, squared, give 16? Both 4² = 16 AND (−4)² = 16 — so x² = 16 has TWO solutions: x = 4 or x = −4, written x = ±4.
Move both x-intercepts until the graph represents x² = 25.

widget.prompt: Build the graph of y = x² − 25 by placing its two crossings. Each crossing is a solution of x² = 25.
widget.successFeedback: The graph crosses at −5 and 5. Both values square to 25, so x² = 25 has two solutions.
widget.shapeFeedback: Set the leading coefficient to 1 so the graph represents x² − 25 rather than a stretched version.
widget.vertexFeedback: Move the two crossings to equal distances on opposite sides of zero: −5 and 5.

predict.prompt: Before moving the crossings, can a negative number squared equal 25?

options.label: Yes; a negative times itself is positive
No; squaring keeps a number negative
Only zero can square to a positive number

predict.reveal: A negative times a negative is positive. Therefore (−5)² and 5² both equal 25, which the two graph crossings make visible.

steps.body: Squaring a positive OR a negative number always gives a positive result (a negative times itself flips back to positive). That's WHY every positive p in x² = p has two solutions, one positive and one negative, that are opposites of each other.

explanationVariants: 7² = 49 and (−7)² = 49, so x² = 49 has solutions x = 7 or x = −7.
Since squaring erases the sign, both 7 and −7 are valid solutions.

commonBuilds.feedback: −7 also works: (−7)² = 49 — don't drop the negative solution.
That's half of 49, not a square root — check 24.5² (much bigger than 49).
49² is way more than 49 — this isn't a solution at all.

widget.missFeedback: Square roots come in ± pairs: both 7² and (−7)² equal 49.

steps.body: x² = p (for positive p) always has TWO solutions: the positive and negative square root.
takeaways: Squaring erases sign, so both +√p and −√p solve x² = p.
√p alone gives just the positive root; solving x²=p wants both signs.
This only works when p is a perfect square here — otherwise the roots are irrational (recall Chapter 2 of the last course!).
steps.teaser: Next: cube roots — where the story is surprisingly different.

concept.body: Solving x² = p (p a positive perfect square) has TWO solutions: the positive square root AND its negative, since both square to the same positive p.
